title: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Like other fluid bodies, its surface, whatsoever other substance, gas, liquid or solid, it be in contact with, and in varying degree according to the nature of that adjacent substance, is the seat of molecular force exhibiting itself as a surface-tension, from the action of which many important consequences follow, which greatly affect the form of the fluid surface.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter I, “Introductory”; topic “Physical properties of the Amoeba”. Scope: fluid or semi-fluid cells such as Amoeba

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch01-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim has measurable variables and perturbation-based tests, but public datasets rarely contain tension, medium and shape together. Available imaging can resolve the shape component and selected mechanisms, not the full causal generalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure amoeboid cell boundary curvature and shape as the contacting medium changes, estimate cortical or interfacial tension, and test whether tension predicts the deformation after controlling for active cytoskeletal forces. A reproducible medium-dependent tension-shape relation would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most image datasets lack independent force measurements.

Historical surface tension maps imperfectly to active cortical tension.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.35
data existence: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The form of an amoeboid cell and its response to boundary stress are measurable, and a perturbation result would discriminate indifference to surface force from a strong effect. The mapping from classical surface tension to cortical tension is standard but not identical, which lowers operationalizability, and the tension values needed for the test have to be compiled. Image repositories cover shape for a useful but narrow set of cells.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat cortical tension as the modern stand-in for Thompson's interfacial tension, then relate measured boundary stress in amoeboid cells to outline curvature. The claim is favored if lowering that stress produces the protrusions and loss of rounding it requires, and weakened if shape is indifferent to boundary stress.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Paired tension-and-shape series sit in paper supplements rather than in the image archives.

Cortical tension is an active regulated stress, not the passive surface tension of a fluid interface.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.55
data existence: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.4
